title: At home
goal: Name rooms and furniture, describe where you live, and share out the housework.
bekal: name all the rooms and the most common furniture
describe a home or room with *badago*, *daude*, and place words
share out housework with *behar dut* and *nik … dut, zuk … duzu*

dialogs.title: Elkarrizketa — Pisua garbitzen
dialogs.intro: Saturday morning in the apartment. Unai stands in the middle of the living room, hands on his hips.

lines.speaker: Unai:
lines.id: Budi, the apartment is pretty dirty.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Egia da. Gaur garbitu behar dugu.
lines.id: That's true. We have to clean today.

lines.text: Nik sukaldea garbitzen dut. Zuk komuna?

notes: **Pisua means apartment, not floor.** All over the region people call their home *pisua* (from Spanish *piso*), or *etxebizitza* in more formal language. *Etxea* is used both for a house and for "home" as the place you go back to.

**Biok — the two of us.** Basque has special words for groups of a set size: *biok* (the two of us), *hirurok* (the three of us), *denok* (all of us), *zuek biok* (you two). These words also show that the speaker is part of the group.

**Liburuz beteta — full of what.** The ending *-z* you know from means of transport also means "with": *liburuz beteta* (full of books), *jendez beteta* (full of people), *urez beteta* (full of water). The order is the reverse of English: the contents first, then "full".

**Nik … dut, zuk … duzu — sharing out tasks.** Since the auxiliary already shows who does it, adding *nik* and *zuk* in front stresses the split: "**I**'ll take the kitchen, **you** take the bathroom". Without that stress, the pronouns are simply dropped.

sections.title: Rooms and parts of the house

blocks.text: Notice the ending *-gela*, meaning "room" — the Latin word *cella* you met in the opening chapter: *lo**gela*** (sleeping room), *jan**gela*** (eating room), *bainu**gela*** (bath room), *ikas**gela*** (classroom). Once you see the pattern, half of the house vocabulary comes for free.

blocks.title: Baserria — the Basque farmhouse
items: A *baserria* is a traditional farmhouse: one big stone building with the animals downstairs and the family above. It's more than a house — it's also a family name. Many Basque surnames are farmhouse names (*Etxeberria* = new house, *Elizalde* = by the church, *Mendizabal* = wide mountain).
*Baserritarra* means someone who lives on a baserri, and at the town market it means a farmer selling their own produce.
When you read a Basque street name or surname, you're almost always reading a description of a place: *etxe* (house), *mendi* (mountain), *ibai* (river), *zabal* (wide), *berri* (new), *zahar* (old).

blocks.text: *Sukaldea* means both the kitchen and the stove, depending on the sentence — a bit like "the range" can mean a whole cooker. To be precise, the stove is *sukalde-plaka* or simply *su* ("fire").

blocks.title: Describing where you live
items: *Nire pisuak hiru logela ditu.* — My apartment has three bedrooms.
*Sukaldea txikia da baina argitsua.* — The kitchen is small but bright.
*Bigarren solairuan bizi naiz.* — I live on the second floor.
*Balkoitik itsasoa ikusten da.* — You can see the sea from the balcony.
*Alokairua garestia da Bilbon.* — Rent is expensive in Bilbo.

blocks.text: To share out tasks, just combine the doer wearing its hat (*nik*) with *behar dut*: *Nik platerak garbitu behar ditut* (I have to do the dishes). Notice that the auxiliary is plural too because there are many plates — *ditut*, not *dut*.

blocks.title: Looking for a place to live
items: *Logela bat alokatu nahi dut.* — I'd like to rent a room.
*Zenbat da hilean?* — How much is it per month?
In Bilbo and Donostia, room ads are usually written in Spanish; but asking a Basque-speaking owner about it in euskara often makes the conversation much warmer.
